holidays.name: Festivus
holidays.description: The "holiday for the rest of us." Celebrate with an unadorned aluminum pole, a dinner table of grievances, and feats of strength that end only when someone gets pinned. It is the perfect antidote to tinsel-fatigue.
holidays.origin: Writer Daniel O'Keefe invented Festivus in the 1960s as a family tradition. His son Dan, a TV writer, brought it to a wide audience in a 1997 Seinfeld episode, "The Strike."
holidays.funFact: The Festivus pole is aluminum because, as the show's Frank Costanza explained, it has a very high strength-to-weight ratio. The real-life O'Keefe family tradition reportedly began with a clock in a bag instead.

holidays.name: National Pfeffernusse Day
holidays.description: A day to enjoy pfeffernüsse, the spicy, powdery little German holiday cookies. They are flavored with cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, and often a pinch of black pepper. Pop a few in your mouth and let the powdered sugar fly.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food observance of unclear origin. The cookies themselves date back centuries in Germany, the Netherlands, and Denmark, where they are a Christmas season staple.
holidays.funFact: The name roughly translates to "pepper nuts." Early versions got their kick from real pepper, which was a pricey, fancy spice in medieval Europe.

holidays.name: Metric Conversion Day
holidays.description: A nod to the measuring system that most of the world uses and that Americans keep politely ignoring. It is a good day to convert your recipe, your commute, or your height into centimeters just for fun.
holidays.origin: The date is tied to the Metric Conversion Act, which was signed into U.S. law on December 23, 1975. It set a national policy of encouraging, but not requiring, a switch to the metric system.
holidays.funFact: The 1975 law created the U.S. Metric Board to coordinate a voluntary switch. The U.S. is still one of very few countries that mostly sticks with miles, pounds, and gallons.
